thing; it is the simplest object on earth, yet one of the most
incomprehensible. If you take two sticks of equal length and equal
weight, each with a small handle attached to one end, and tie them so
that they point in exactly opposite directions, you will have invented
the broom. Yet I believe that this simple instrument was originally
invented by men who could not even see straight. When I see the broom

or any of the other instruments of gardening. When I think of the broom
I think of something more than a rake, or a spade, or any of the other
instruments of gardening. When I see the broom, I feel the wind blowing
against my face.

And when I look at the broom I wonder why the wind should blow against
my face. For surely the broom, if it is to be effective, must be
facing away from the wind; just as the rake or the spade must be facing
away from the soil. Yet if the broom does not face away from the wind,
it is useless. So long as the wind is blowing towards the broom it is
ineffective. But when the wind begins to blow against it, when it has
blown itself into existence, it is then only then that the broom
begins to work.
